"Discrimination" has two distinct meanings that are both in active use today. Understanding both is essential, because using or hearing the word without knowing which meaning is intended can lead to real confusion.
Meaning 1 — The Neutral Sense: Noticing Differences

"Discrimination" simply means the ability to recognize and tell apart differences between things. This is the older, more neutral sense of the word, and it carries no judgment — it is actually a sign of intelligence and sharpness.

When used this way, it means a kind of careful, precise perception — the skill of noticing subtle distinctions that others might miss.

Examples:

  • A professional wine taster has a discrimination of flavors that most people lack. (She can tell a wine from France apart from one from Italy just by taste.)
  • A skilled editor has a discrimination for language — she can spot awkward phrasing that looks perfectly fine to others.
  • "His discrimination in choosing art for the gallery is remarkable." (He picks pieces with a trained, careful eye.)

When someone is called "a discriminating person" in this sense, it is a compliment. It means they have refined, exacting taste and judgment — they don't accept just anything.
Meaning 2 — The Social Sense: Unfair Treatment of People

This is the meaning most people think of today, and it is the far more common one in everyday conversation. Here, "discrimination" means treating a person or group of people unfairly or unequally because of who they are, not because of anything they have actually done or earned.

The key idea: a person is judged not on their own merits, actions, or abilities, but on a characteristic they belong to — such as their race, gender, religion, age, disability, nationality, sexual orientation, or social class.

Examples:

  • A company refuses to hire a qualified woman simply because she is a woman. That is gender discrimination.
  • A landlord refuses to rent to a family because of their religion. That is religious discrimination.
  • A person is paid less than a colleague doing the same job, purely because of their skin color. That is racial discrimination.
  • An older employee is passed over for promotion only because of their age. That is age discrimination.

In all of these cases, the characteristic being used (gender, religion, race, age) has nothing to do with the person's ability to do the job or meet the requirement. That is what makes it discrimination — the judgment is irrelevant and unfair.
The Different Forms Discrimination Can Take

Discrimination in this social sense doesn't always show up in an obvious, direct way. It can be subtle or even unintentional:

Direct discrimination is the most straightforward kind. Someone is treated worse than others explicitly because of a characteristic. "We don't hire people from that community" is direct discrimination stated openly.

Indirect discrimination is trickier. A rule or policy applies equally to everyone on the surface, but in practice it puts a particular group at a significant disadvantage — and there is no good reason for it. For example: a company requires all employees to work on Sundays with no exceptions. This seems neutral, but it puts Christians (for whom Sunday is a day of worship) at a disadvantage that doesn't apply to others.

Systemic or institutional discrimination is when discrimination is baked into the way an entire system, organization, or society operates — not just one person's attitude. It means the structures and rules themselves produce unequal outcomes for certain groups, even when no single person may be acting with conscious prejudice.

You may sometimes hear the phrase positive discrimination (in British English) or affirmative action (in American English). This refers to deliberately favoring a group that has historically been disadvantaged or underrepresented — for example, giving preference in hiring or university admissions to people from marginalized backgrounds. The intention is to correct existing inequality.

This is controversial: supporters argue it is a necessary tool to level an uneven playing field; critics argue that favoring one group over another, even with good intentions, is itself a form of unfairness. The word "positive" here is used to signal the intent is corrective rather than harmful — though whether it is actually "positive" is a matter of genuine debate.
The Critical Distinction Between the Two Meanings

Here is the clearest way to hold both meanings in your mind at once:

  • In Meaning 1, you are discriminating between things — wine, art, arguments, quality. You are using your judgment to tell apart what is good from what is poor, based on relevant qualities. This is a skill, and it is good.
  • In Meaning 2, you are discriminating against people — treating them worse based on characteristics like race or gender that are irrelevant to the situation at hand. This is a harm, and it is unjust.

The shared thread is the idea of drawing a distinction. But in Meaning 1, the distinction is made carefully and fairly, based on what actually matters. In Meaning 2, the distinction is made unjustly, based on what doesn't matter.
A Final Note on Degree and Context

Discrimination in the social sense exists on a spectrum. It can be:

  • Overt — openly stated, aggressive, and intentional
  • Subtle — hidden in microaggressions, assumptions, or tone
  • Unconscious (implicit bias) — when a person discriminates without being fully aware that they are doing so; their deep-seated assumptions shape their behavior without their conscious knowledge

Discrimination also matters legally. In most democratic countries, discrimination on the basis of race, gender, religion, disability, and several other characteristics is illegal in employment, housing, and public services. This is why the word appears so often in law, journalism, and public policy discussions.

In short: discrimination either means the sharp ability to tell things apart (a positive quality of mind) or the unfair treatment of people based on irrelevant characteristics (a social wrong). Context — especially whether the subject is a person being treated a certain way or a quality someone possesses — almost always makes clear which meaning is intended.
